title: Could AI Have Discovered Fatigue? A Historical Thought Experiment on Prediction, Mechanism, and the Scientist’s Role
content: Could an artificial intelligence (AI) system have recognised material fatigue before engineers had named and systematically investigated it? This counterfactual question provides a demanding test of the distinction between successful prediction and physical explanation. Here, we construct a historically bounded thought experiment using early writings on strength and elasticity, while recognising an important complication: Tredgold [1] had already described fracture under repeated flexure in 1822, decades before the later systematic development of fatigue research. Any apparent rediscovery of fatigue by a present-day language model therefore cannot, by itself, be regarded as independent scientific discovery. We instead formulate an auditable test in which an AI system must recognise an anomalous failure, distinguish among competing explanations, propose experiments capable of discriminating between them, and make prospective predictions without access to the later conceptual solution. The purpose is not to claim that contemporary AI has failed such a test, but to clarify what evidence would be required before attributing genuine physical discovery to an AI system. The broader implication is that computational prediction can substantially extend scientific capability, whereas experimentally accountable interpretation remains a central component of scientific understanding.
